title: Evaluating a Generate–Validate–Repair Pipeline for LLM‑based Network Configuration: a Paired, Emulation‑Grounded Study
abstract: We preregistered and executed a paired, emulation‑grounded experiment (study id study-cand-1-gvr-verifier-adversarial-2026-08-01) to evaluate whether integrating a deterministic network verifier into a generate–validate–repair (GVR) pipeline reduces the rate of unsafe configuration applications from an LLM relative to an LLM‑only pipeline. Execution used the declared model gpt-5-mini and deterministic_netops_validator_v5 under shared_initial_candidate semantics (exactly one initial LLM generation per task, reused across arms); guarded episodes could request up to one validator‑triggered repair. We ran N = 240 paired intent→configuration tasks (144 in‑distribution, 48 distribution‑shift, 48 adversarial). Every paired episode was scored safe under both arms (baseline = 240/240 safe; guarded = 240/240 safe). The paired risk difference (guarded − baseline) = 0.00; 95% bootstrap percentile CI = [0.00, 0.00] (10,000 resamples, seed = 1729); exact McNemar two‑sided p = 1.0. Under the preregistered shared_initial_candidate semantics the single shared generation per task passed deterministic validation in every case, so no validator‑triggered repairs were invoked and the paired contrast is degenerate. We present the preregistered design, artifact‑grounded execution accounting, quantitative analysis, an evidence‑based failure analysis explaining the null paired outcome, and concrete recommendations for future informative GVR evaluations.

sections.introduction:
Translating high‑level operator intent into safe device configurations is a central NetOps challenge. Large language models (LLMs) can generate plausible configuration sequences from natural language, but textual fidelity alone does not guarantee operational safety: ordering errors, transient invariants, and protected‑resource touches can produce outages when configurations are applied. Deterministic, execution‑grounded evaluation—where candidate configurations are validated against emulated device state and semantic invariants—exposes these operational failure modes in a way that token‑level benchmarks do not [1].

A common architectural pattern to improve safety is generate–validate–repair (GVR): an LLM proposes a candidate configuration, a deterministic verifier checks semantic invariants, and an automated repair routine rewrites the candidate when violations are detected. Prior work documents GVR‑style designs across program repair and configuration domains and reports strong gains on many syntactic and constrained semantic faults, but open questions remain about how much verifier integration reduces unsafe applications under distribution shift and adversarial prompts, and about experimental designs that produce informative paired contrasts between guarded and unguarded pipelines [2],[3],[4].

This paper reports a fully preregistered paired experiment that measured a single, precisely defined estimand: the absolute paired difference in unsafe_apply rate (guarded − baseline). The experiment used shared_initial_candidate semantics (a single initial LLM generation per task, reused across both arms) so that any paired difference could only arise if the shared candidate failed deterministic validation or if the guarded arm applied a validator‑triggered repair. The empirical outcome was degenerate (no discordant pairs). We preserve and reference the archived execution and analysis artifacts to explain why the paired contrast was null and to derive concrete recommendations for future, informative GVR evaluations.
sections.related_work:
Executable, emulation‑grounded benchmarks have been proposed to surface workflow and planning faults for LLM agents rather than only assessing textual fidelity; recent work develops closed‑loop testbeds that execute generated configurations and score semantic outcomes [1]. Automatic configuration and program repair literature documents generate–validate patterns and shows that deterministic validators often enable high repair coverage for a range of benchmarked faults, while also noting that verifier coverage and repair search strategy constrain effectiveness [2],[4]. Surveys and position papers synthesize agentic architectures, tool augmentation, and verifier integration as promising for operational automation and safety [3],[5]. The evolution of configuration analysis tools such as Batfish provides engineering precedent for verifier design and incremental verification in production toolchains [6].

Our study differs in three respects: (i) a preregistered paired estimand explicitly mapping to archived analysis artifacts; (ii) enforced shared_initial_candidate semantics that make the causal contrast dependent on validator detection and repair; and (iii) closed‑loop emulation scoring that deterministically defines unsafe_apply versus safe_apply outcomes. These design choices produce a narrowly interpretable estimand and a tightly auditable execution record useful for failure‑analytic insights.
sections.methodology:
Preregistration and estimand: We preregistered the study (study id study-cand-1-gvr-verifier-adversarial-2026-08-01) and specified the primary estimand as paired_success_rate_difference_guarded_minus_baseline: the absolute paired difference in unsafe_apply rate (guarded − baseline), where unsafe_apply = 1 denotes a final configuration that would cause a semantic safety violation when applied in the emulator. The primary analysis uses a paired contingency approach with bootstrap percentile confidence intervals and an exact McNemar test.

Design and generation semantics: The experiment used a paired design with exactly N = 240 distinct intent→configuration tasks. Task composition: in‑distribution = 144, distribution‑shift = 48, adversarial‑prompt = 48. Crucially, the registered adapter implemented shared_initial_candidate semantics: for each task the system produced a single initial LLM generation and both arms observed that same candidate; the guarded arm could request at most one validator‑triggered repair. Under this contract, paired differences can only arise when the shared initial candidate fails validation or when a single repair alters the guarded final output relative to baseline.

Model, verifier, and budget constraints: Execution declared the single hosted model gpt-5-mini and used a deterministic semantic checker (deterministic_netops_validator_v5). The guarded pipeline permitted up to one validator‑triggered repair per task. The planned maximum model‑call budget matched the paired design and the shared_initial_candidate semantics (one initial generation per task).

Scoring and exclusion rules: Final outcomes were binary: safe (0) or unsafe (1) as determined by deterministic execution of the generated configuration in the emulated device state and by invariant checks. The preregistration specified deterministic flagging rules: if the verifier reported PASS but the emulator observed an unsafe outcome, the pair would be flagged as 'possible false‑safe' and excluded from the primary analysis (included in sensitivity analyses). Infrastructure failures after allowed retries would be excluded as infra failures and reported separately. The retry policy allowed up to two recovery attempts for technical errors.
sections.results:
Execution accounting: The run completed under the preregistered plan: N = 240 pairs (planned episodes = 480; completed episodes = 480). Provider calls conformed to the shared_initial_candidate contract (one initial LLM generation per task) and the guarded repair budget was unused because no validation failure triggered a repair. No infra failures or preregistered exclusions occurred.

Primary outcomes and statistical summary: Every paired episode was scored safe under both arms. Observed counts: n11 (both safe) = 240; n10 = 0; n01 = 0; n00 = 0. Therefore baseline unsafe_apply rate = 0/240 = 0.0 and guarded unsafe_apply rate = 0/240 = 0.0. The paired risk difference (guarded − baseline) = 0.00. Bootstrap percentile 95% CI using 10,000 resamples (seed = 1729) is [0.00, 0.00]. The exact McNemar two‑sided test yields p = 1.0. These results follow directly from the preregistered estimand mapping and the deterministic scoring rules.

Validator activity and repair budget utilization: Deterministic validation passed every shared candidate; accordingly, zero validator‑triggered repairs were applied in the guarded arm. Planned secondary diagnostics (median repair iteration count, model‑call budget per task) are degenerate in this run: repair iterations = 0 for all guarded episodes; model calls per task were equal to one shared generation under the registered semantics.

Planned sensitivity channels: The preregistration included sensitivity analyses treating flagged 'possible false‑safe' items or infra‑failed pairs as unsafe in worst‑case analyses. No items were flagged and no infra failures occurred, so these sensitivity analyses are vacuous for this execution.
sections.discussion:
Mechanistic explanation for the null paired contrast: Under the shared_initial_candidate semantics the paired contrast depends on the single shared LLM generation failing deterministic validation (so guarded can differ by repair) or on the guarded arm applying a repair. In this execution every shared candidate passed validation; thus the guarded arm had no opportunity to apply a repair and could not create discordant pairs. The null paired result is therefore an expected, mechanistically explained outcome of the preregistered generation semantics together with the observed verifier PASS pattern.

Implications for experimental design: Shared_initial_candidate semantics enforce a tightly paired LLM sample and reduce model‑call budget, but they also reduce the chance of observing verifier benefit because they eliminate generator variability between arms. To obtain an informative paired estimate of verifier benefit in future work, one or more of the following should be adopted: (A) permit independent initial generations per arm so the guarded arm can be compared to an independent baseline generation; (B) increase adversary strength or diversity so that some shared candidates fail validation; or (C) enlarge repair budgets (allow multiple repair iterations) and instrument repair search behavior. Each choice trades model‑call budget, reproducibility, and interpretability differently; the present artifact record makes these tradeoffs explicit and measurable.

Threats to validity: Internal validity — the shared_initial_candidate contract is an explicit experimental choice that limits the causal contrast to validator detection and repair; this constraint must be considered when interpreting a null paired difference. Construct validity — deterministic validators implement a finite set of checks and can fail to capture unencoded semantic fault classes; planned cross‑checks between validator PASS and emulator outcomes are a necessary safeguard for false‑safe detection in broader deployments. External validity — tasks were drawn from a synthetic emulation corpus; extrapolation to production, multi‑vendor deployments and operator procedures requires additional evaluation. Conclusion validity — realized baseline unsafe rate = 0 in this run prevents detection of verifier benefit under the current design and adversary strength; future power planning should incorporate generator variability or stronger adversaries to induce informative discordant pairs.
sections.conclusion:
We executed a fully preregistered, paired, emulation‑grounded evaluation of a generate–validate–repair pipeline for LLM‑based network configuration. Observed outcome: all 240 pairs were safe under both arms, yielding a paired difference = 0.00 (95% bootstrap CI [0.00, 0.00]; McNemar p = 1.0). This degenerate outcome is directly traceable to the preregistered shared_initial_candidate semantics together with deterministic validator PASS on every shared candidate: because the guarded arm could only alter the final output via a validator‑triggered repair and no repairs were invoked, no discordant pairs could arise. We therefore emphasize that experimental semantics (shared vs independent generation), adversary strength, and repair budget are critical design knobs for producing informative paired contrasts when evaluating GVR pipelines. Future work should deliberately choose generation semantics and adversary protocols to ensure the primary estimand has opportunity to vary and should expand verifier coverage and repair instrumentation to study repair behavior under realistic failure modes.

The study was preregistered (study id study-cand-1-gvr-verifier-adversarial-2026-08-01; preregistration SHA‑256: 3e73ca0dc935a8754bf2dfbe6869ff989c47f1db0d93e2ca34809be8ebf95e26) and executed under the frozen plan after the autonomy lock. No manual human editing of technical manuscript content occurred after the autonomy lock.
limitations: Emulation and corpus scope: tasks were drawn from a synthetic, emulation‑grounded corpus; external validity to production, multi‑vendor operations and operator workflows is limited.
Single model: evaluation used a single declared model (gpt‑5‑mini); results do not imply generality across models, prompt templates, or provider implementations.

Generation semantics: the shared_initial_candidate design (single shared generation per task) constrains causal interpretation because it prevents generator variability between arms and therefore reduces opportunities for verifier benefit to manifest.
Adversary bounds: adversarial prompts were generated under a preregistered, fixed protocol and do not represent unconstrained adaptive adversaries.

Verifier coverage: deterministic_netops_validator_v5 implements a finite set of checks; semantic fault classes outside that coverage could remain undetected and require expanded validator specifications and cross‑checks.
